title: Balak Hires Balaam, and a Donkey Sees the Angel
summary: As Israel camps on the plains of Moab, King Balak, terrified by their numbers, sends for Balaam son of Beor, a famous diviner from near the Euphrates, to curse them. God first forbids Balaam to go, then allows him to go on the condition that he speaks only what God tells him. On the road the angel of the LORD blocks his way three times; Balaam's donkey sees the angel and turns aside, Balaam beats her, and God opens her mouth to speak before opening Balaam's eyes.
story: Israel has reached the last stopping place before the promised land, the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho, where it will remain for the rest of the book and all of Deuteronomy. Chapters 22 to 24, the story of Balaam, are unusual in the Bible: for most of the story Israel is offstage, unaware that a foreign king and a hired seer are plotting against them on the hills above. The story answers a question left hanging after all of Israel's grumbling in the wilderness: has God given up on his people? The answer, spoken through the mouth of an outsider hired to curse them, is that the blessing God promised Abraham still stands. The donkey episode in this chapter prepares for that answer by showing that God can make even a donkey speak, and so he can make a diviner bless.
historical:
Balak, son of Zippor, is king of Moab, the people living east of the Dead Sea, and he has just watched Israel defeat Sihon and Og to his north (Numbers 21). The elders of Midian are also involved (verses 4 and 7). The Midianites were a loose group of peoples linked to the deserts east and south, and they reappear in chapters 25 and 31. Balaam lives at Pethor, “by the Euphrates”, a long trip of several hundred miles; some scholars connect Pethor with a town called Pitru mentioned in Assyrian records, though the identification is not certain.

Balaam is one of the few figures in the Pentateuch attested outside the Bible. In 1967, excavators at Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley found fragments of an inscription written in ink on a plastered wall, usually dated to around the eighth century BC. It tells of a vision of the gods given to Balaam son of Beor, who is called a seer of the gods. The text does not describe the events of Numbers, but it shows that Balaam was remembered in the region as a famous seer for centuries.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, many believed that professional diviners and curse-speakers could manipulate the gods and bind the future with their words. Kings hired them before battle, and curses were taken seriously as real weapons. Balak's words in verse 6 express that belief exactly: “those you bless are blessed, and those you curse are cursed”. The fees for divination (verse 7) show that this was a paid profession. Divination (qesem) was forbidden to Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10), and the story shows why: blessing and curse belong to God, not to a hired expert.

The donkey was the ordinary riding animal for travel, and a trusted donkey could be a man's companion for years, as this one points out (verse 30). The humor of the scene would not have been lost on first readers. Balaam, the famous seer who claims to see the gods, is the only one on the road who cannot see the angel, while his donkey sees him three times. He threatens to kill her with a sword he does not have (verse 29), while the angel standing before him holds one drawn.
literary: The chapter is built with repeated patterns, especially threes. There are two embassies from Balak, the second larger and more honored than the first. On the road the angel stands three times, each time in a narrower place: first in the road with room to go into a field, then in a passage between vineyard walls, then in a place with no room to turn at all. Balaam beats the donkey three times. The word for opposing Balaam in verses 22 and 32 is satan, which here is not a name but a common noun meaning an adversary. The story is full of irony: the seer is blind, the donkey sees, and the man hired to control the gods with words cannot even control his own animal. The chapter's key line is repeated in different forms: Balaam may speak only what God tells him (verses 20, 35, and 38).

outline.t: Balak fears Israel and sends for Balaam
The first embassy: God forbids Balaam to go
The second embassy: God permits him to go and speak only his word
The angel, the donkey, and Balaam's opened eyes
Balak meets Balaam and takes him to Bamoth-baal

doctrines.note: God controls the whole story: he speaks to a foreign diviner, opens a donkey's mouth, and blocks a road. Kings and seers make plans, but God decides what will be spoken over his people.

Balak's belief that Balaam's word determines blessing and curse is answered by God's own words: “they are blessed” (verse 12). God's promise to Abraham to bless those who bless his descendants stands behind the whole story.
God reveals himself even to an outsider, but on his own terms. Balaam must speak only what God puts in his mouth, a phrase later used of Israel's true prophets.

words.note: Arar, to curse, to bind under a curse. Balak's whole plan rests on it. The story's point is that no human curse can stand against God's blessing, a theme that runs through the next two chapters.

Barak, to bless. God tells Balaam that Israel is blessed (verse 12). The word recalls God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3, and the Balaam story shows that promise being kept even through a hostile outsider.

Satan, adversary or opponent. In verses 22 and 32 it describes the angel of the LORD standing against Balaam, which shows the word's ordinary meaning. Only later in the Old Testament does it begin to function as a title for a particular accuser (Job 1 and Zechariah 3).

Qesem, divination, the practice of seeking hidden knowledge or influencing events through omens and rituals. The elders bring fees for it. Deuteronomy 18:10 forbids it in Israel, and this story shows it is powerless against God's purposes.

christ: The Balaam story matters for the story leading to Jesus because it confirms that God's promise to bless Abraham's descendants, and through them all nations (Genesis 12:3), cannot be overturned by any enemy. That promise is the line along which the Bible traces the coming of the Messiah, and Balaam's later oracles will speak of a star and a scepter rising from Israel (Numbers 24:17). The angel of the LORD who stands in the road has been understood by some Christian interpreters as an appearance of the Son of God before his incarnation, because the angel speaks with God's own authority; others hold that he is a created angel sent as God's messenger, and the text does not settle the question. The New Testament uses Balaam as a warning against those who serve God for profit (2 Peter 2:15-16; Jude 11), and it contrasts such figures with Christ, who did not come to be enriched but to give himself.

hard.q: Why does God tell Balaam to go and then become angry when he goes?
hard.a:
Verse 20 says God told Balaam to go with the men, and verse 22 says God's anger was kindled because he went. Interpreters offer several explanations. One is that God's permission was conditional (go, but only do what I tell you), and Balaam set out with a heart already set on the reward and on finding a way to curse, which the angel calls a perverse way (verse 32). Another is that Balaam should never have asked a second time after God's clear first answer (verse 12); by asking again, he showed that he hoped God would change his mind, and God gave him what he wanted along with a warning. A third view, held by many critical scholars, is that the donkey story was originally a separate tradition placed here, which accounts for the tension; even on this view the final text invites the reader to see a gap between Balaam's words and his desires.

The New Testament's later judgment points in the direction of the first two explanations. It remembers Balaam as a man who loved the wages of wrongdoing (2 Peter 2:15), even though in this chapter he says the right things about obeying God.

questions: Balaam said all the right things about obeying God while hoping for Balak's reward. Where might your words about God and your real desires be pulling in different directions?
The donkey saw what the famous seer could not. Who in your life might be seeing something clearly that you are missing?
Balak believed that a curse could undo what God had blessed. What fears or voices make you doubt that God's promises to you still stand?
